newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - US Senate set to act on last of S&L crisis.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - US Senate set to act on last of S&L crisis.

text.p: The Senate was poised to pass legislation Monday putting to rest the lingering hangover of the savings and loan crisis.
The House passed the so-called "BIF-SAIF" measure Saturday as part of a broader budget bill that is now in the hands of the Senate where a vote was expected late in the day.
"It looks like today will be the day it gets through the Senate," Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke said.
The Bank Insurance Fund (BIF) and the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF) insure deposits at banks and thrifts respectively.

The BIF had reached the mandated level of $1.25 for every $100 of insured deposits, while the SAIF was still years away. Consequently banks saw their premiums drop to essentially zero while thrifts continued to pay 23 cents per $100 of deposits.
SAIF growth was slowed by making annual interest payments on Financing Corp (FICO) bonds issued in the late 1980s to help with clean-up costs for hundreds of failed thrifts.

The BIF-SAIF measure would require the thrift industry to pay a one-time charge of $4.7 billion to boost the SAIF to the required level, after which thrifts and banks would share the FICO interest payments.

The formula for the sharing would require thrifts to pay $458 million and banks to pay $322 million a year for three years starting Jan. 1, 1997. The remaining $13 million of the $793 million annual interest payment comes from interest income due to the FICO payment schedule.
Starting Jan. 1, 2000 through 2017 there would be pro rata cost-sharing with thrifts paying $172 million and banks paying $608 million a year through premiums.
Regulators had warned of a potential default on FICO bonds if steps were not taken to bolster the SAIF.
"We are enormously pleased that the last vestiges of the problems with the thrift industry have now been solved," without using taxpayer funds, Hawke said.
Banks viewed BIF-SAIF as an unwarranted "tax" on their industry and would have opposed the measure if other provisions had not been added such as regulatory relief and lender liability measures.

The lender liability provision would exempt financial institutions from liability if they foreclosed on properties involving hazardous materials, as long as the lender was not involved in managing the property.
Another provision that banks wanted would prevent the Farm Credit system from sponsoring a credit union for its customers, while it could still have one for employees.
Insurance agents who had fought tooth-and-nail to tack on measures making it more difficult for banks to gain ground in insurance did not succeed in the bill that passed the House.
But one provision that the insurance industry had sought was included -- that federal deposit insurance would not cover retirement certificates of deposit.

House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach, R-Iowa, over the weekend said the Republican leadreship intended to address the concerns of the insurance agents in "comprehensive" financial industry reform in the next Congress.

Federal Reserve Governor Susan Phillips said the Fed was "disappointed" that agreement was not reached on Glass-Steagall reform this year. The Glass-Steagall Act, a Depression-era law, separates commercial and investment banking.
"We continue to believe that additional modernization is needed," Phillips said.
